notes: Original 60 taught AS Physics/Chemistry first-mock core recall cards from v323 topic shortlist, excluding earlier v324/v327 samples. One definition expanded to be scientifically specific; retain earlier wording as accepted explanation.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why can a couple turn an object without a resultant force?
records.originalBack: Its two equal, opposite, parallel forces cancel as forces, but act along separate lines to cause turning.
accept: A couple has zero net force because the two forces oppose, but its separated force lines create a turning moment.
reject: A couple produces rotation because its resultant force is nonzero.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: 50 N at 30° above horizontal: find horizontal and vertical components.
records.originalBack: Horizontal = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N; vertical = 50 sin 30° = 25.0 N.
accept: For 50 N at 30 degrees above horizontal, horizontal=43.3 N and vertical=25 N.
reject: The horizontal component is 25 N and the vertical component 43.3 N.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: 50 N at 30° to vertical: find horizontal and vertical components.
records.originalBack: Horizontal = 50 sin 30° = 25.0 N; vertical = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N.
accept: At 30 degrees to vertical, horizontal=25 N and vertical=43.3 N for a 50 N force.
reject: A force 30 degrees to vertical has horizontal=43.3 N and vertical=25 N.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: In motion graphs, what do a gradient and a signed area each represent?
records.originalBack: s–t gradient → v; v–t gradient → a, area → Δs; a–t area → Δv.
accept: s-t slope=v; v-t slope=a and signed area=displacement; a-t signed area=change in velocity.
reject: Area under a displacement-time graph gives acceleration, and slope of a velocity-time graph gives distance.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: A 2.0 kg object accelerates at 3.0 m s⁻². Friction is 4.0 N opposite the pull. Find the pull.
records.originalBack: Resultant force = ma = 6.0 N; pulling force = 6.0+4.0 = 10.0 N.
accept: The resultant must be 2.0 times 3.0=6 N, so applied pull is 6+4=10 N.
reject: The pulling force is only 2 N because the frictional force must be subtracted from ma.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Does the normal reaction always equal an object's weight?
records.originalBack: No, only in certain force balances.
accept: No: on an incline it is mg cos theta when no extra perpendicular forces act.
reject: The normal reaction always equals mg, regardless of slope or other forces.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What stays constant horizontally in ideal projectile motion?
records.originalBack: Velocity; horizontal acceleration is zero.
accept: The horizontal component of velocity stays the same without drag.
reject: Horizontal velocity decreases uniformly because gravity acts downwards.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is the vertical acceleration during ideal projectile motion?
records.originalBack: g downward.
accept: Acceleration is g towards the ground at all points, including the highest point.
reject: Vertical acceleration is zero at the highest point of the projectile.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Ignoring air resistance, what is the horizontal acceleration of a projectile?
records.originalBack: Zero.
accept: The projectile has no horizontal acceleration when drag is neglected.
reject: Horizontal acceleration equals 9.81 m/s squared.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Two equal opposite 15 N forces form a couple separated by 0.40 m. Find the moment.
records.originalBack: Moment of the couple = Fd = 15×0.40 = 6.0 N m. Do not double it.
accept: A couple moment is force times the separation, 15 times 0.4 = 6 N m.
reject: The moment is 12 N m because both forces must be added as moments when using full separation.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How does doubling particle momentum affect de Broglie wavelength?
records.originalBack: It halves the wavelength, since λ = h/p.
accept: Since lambda=h/p, twice the momentum means half the de Broglie wavelength.
reject: Doubling momentum doubles the de Broglie wavelength.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: In an inelastic collision of an isolated system, which quantities are conserved?
records.originalBack: Total momentum is conserved; total kinetic energy need not be conserved.
accept: In an isolated inelastic collision momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy generally is not.
reject: In any inelastic collision both total momentum and total kinetic energy must stay constant.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is an impulse?
records.originalBack: Change in momentum, FΔt.
accept: Impulse is the change of momentum, equal to the area under force-time graph.
reject: Impulse is the same as work done and has units of joules.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Which equation links an electron's de Broglie wavelength λ with its momentum p?
records.originalBack: λ = h/p.
accept: de Broglie wavelength is Planck's constant divided by momentum, lambda=h/p.
reject: Electron wavelength equals the electron momentum multiplied by h.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: A force parallel to motion rises linearly from 0 to 40 N across 2.0 m. Find work done.
records.originalBack: Work = triangular area under F–s graph = ½×2.0×40 = 40 J.
accept: Area under F-distance is a triangle: one-half times 2 times 40 = 40 J.
reject: The work is 80 J because the linearly increasing force must be treated as constant at 40 N.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: An engine exerts a 30 N force along the direction of travel at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Find power.
accept: For force parallel to motion, power=force times speed=120 watts.
reject: Power is 7.5 W from dividing force by speed.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: For a stress–strain graph, when does the gradient give Young modulus?
records.originalBack: In the straight-line elastic region: E = Δstress/Δstrain.
accept: Young modulus is stress-strain slope only over the linear elastic portion.
reject: The stress-strain gradient is Young modulus throughout all plastic deformation.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is tensile stress?
records.originalBack: stress = F/A, in Pa.
accept: Tensile stress is applied tensile force per cross-sectional area, in pascals.
reject: Tensile stress is extension divided by original length and has no units.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why can an element's absorption and emission lines have matching wavelengths?
records.originalBack: The same energy gaps are involved in upward and downward electron transitions.
accept: Absorption and emission can involve the same pair of electron levels, giving equal photon energy gaps.
reject: Absorption and emission lines of an element are unrelated because transitions never share energy levels.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is phase difference?
records.originalBack: The difference in position within an oscillation cycle.
records.revisedBack: The difference in phase angle between two oscillations or points on a wave, measured in radians or degrees.
accept: The angular phase offset between two oscillations, measured in radians or degrees.
reject: Phase difference is the physical distance between two objects irrespective of wavelength.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why do electron diffraction rings shrink as accelerating voltage rises?
records.originalBack: Electrons gain momentum, λ = h/p falls, and diffraction angles decrease.
accept: More accelerating voltage gives electrons greater momentum and shorter wavelength, reducing diffraction angle.
reject: Higher accelerating voltage increases electron de Broglie wavelength and ring radius.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why is the central white-light double-slit fringe white?
records.originalBack: All wavelengths have zero path difference there.
accept: Every wavelength has zero path difference on the centre line, so the superposed light is white.
reject: The central fringe is white because only red light reaches the centre.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How do stationary waves form?
records.originalBack: Two coherent waves travel in opposite directions and superpose.
accept: Two coherent waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions interfere to give fixed nodes and antinodes.
reject: Stationary waves arise when two waves travel in the same direction at different frequencies.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: In string-wave RP1, what controls the fundamental frequency?
records.originalBack: Vibrating length, tension and mass per unit length.
accept: For a fixed-end string, fundamental frequency depends on vibrating length, tension and mass per unit length.
reject: Only the driving amplitude controls a fixed string's fundamental frequency.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What relation can be tested by plotting f² against tension?
records.originalBack: A straight line at fixed length and mass per unit length.
accept: At fixed length and linear density, f squared is directly proportional to tension.
reject: A plot of f squared against tension must be inverse because greater tension lowers frequency.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is refractive index?
records.originalBack: n = c/v for light in the medium.
accept: Refractive index is speed in vacuum divided by speed in the medium.
reject: Refractive index is medium light speed divided by c.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What happens to light wavelength on entering a higher-index medium?
records.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: Light frequency stays constant, so lower speed in a higher-index medium means shorter wavelength.
reject: The frequency must increase to explain the shorter wavelength in glass.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is the gradient of a graph of maximum photoelectron KE against frequency?
records.originalBack: Planck constant, h.
accept: The slope of maximum kinetic energy versus incident light frequency is h.
reject: The slope equals work function phi, with units of joules.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How do baryons and mesons differ?
records.originalBack: Baryons contain three quarks; mesons contain a quark and an antiquark.
accept: Baryons have three quarks, while mesons contain a quark and an antiquark.
reject: A meson is a hadron made from three quarks, while a baryon is quark-antiquark.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why should current not be left flowing unnecessarily in a cell experiment?
records.originalBack: Heating and changing cell conditions can alter measurements.
accept: Leaving current flowing heats the cell and changes its conditions, distorting terminal pd/internal-resistance readings.
reject: A current left running cannot affect emf or terminal potential difference measurements.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How do you calculate Ar from two isotope abundances?
records.originalBack: (isotope mass₁×abundance₁ + mass₂×abundance₂) ÷ total abundance.
accept: Multiply each isotope's mass by its fractional abundance and add the products.
reject: Take the simple unweighted mean of isotope masses regardless of abundances.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why is Ar of an isotope mixture a weighted mean?
records.originalBack: More abundant isotopes contribute more to the average mass.
accept: An isotope with higher relative abundance contributes more strongly to average atomic mass.
reject: Each isotope makes the same contribution regardless of its abundance.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is formed by electron-impact ionisation of X(g)?
records.originalBack: X⁺(g), after an electron is removed.
accept: An electron is removed to give the gaseous positive ion X+ and an electron.
reject: Electron-impact ionisation directly forms a negative ion X- by adding an electron.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why do successive ionisation energies increase?
records.originalBack: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.
accept: As each electron is removed the ion becomes more positive, increasing attraction to the remaining electrons.
reject: Successive ionisation energies fall because the increasingly positive ion attracts electrons less.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How many shared pairs are in a double and a triple covalent bond?
records.originalBack: Two and three shared electron pairs respectively.
accept: A double covalent bond consists of two shared electron pairs and a triple bond of three.
reject: A double bond shares four electron pairs and a triple shares six.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Which species donates the lone pair in NH₃→BF₃?
records.originalBack: The nitrogen atom in NH₃ donates to electron-deficient boron in BF₃.
accept: The nitrogen lone pair in NH3 forms the dative bond to boron in BF3.
reject: BF3 nitrogen donates a lone pair to ammonia.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why does diamond have an extremely high melting point?
records.originalBack: Many strong covalent C–C bonds throughout the giant lattice must be broken.
accept: Many strong covalent bonds throughout the diamond structure require substantial energy to break.
reject: Diamond melts at low temperature because it has only weak intermolecular forces between molecules.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does graphite's bonding look like?
records.originalBack: Each C forms three covalent bonds in layers of hexagonal rings; one electron is delocalised.
accept: Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others in hexagonal layers, leaving a delocalised electron.
reject: Graphite consists of isolated tetrahedral carbon molecules with no free electrons.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is an ionic lattice?
records.originalBack: A giant 3D repeating arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attractions.
accept: A three-dimensional regular repeating giant structure of positive and negative ions.
reject: An ionic lattice is a set of separate small molecules held by covalent bonds.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What happens to a Hess enthalpy when the equation is halved?
records.originalBack: Halve the ΔH value.
accept: If every stoichiometric coefficient is halved, the enthalpy change is halved too.
reject: Halving the reaction coefficients doubles the reaction enthalpy change.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why does first IE fall down Group 2?
records.originalBack: Outer electrons are farther away and more shielded, despite a larger nuclear charge.
accept: Greater outer-shell distance and shielding outweigh the increasing nuclear charge down Group 2.
reject: First ionisation energy falls down Group 2 because nuclear charge decreases down the group.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What forms when a Group 2 metal reacts with water?
records.originalBack: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen.
accept: A Group 2 metal reacts with water to give a metal hydroxide and H2.
reject: Group 2 metals react with water to form only a metal oxide and oxygen.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What colour precipitate indicates bromide with silver ions?
records.originalBack: Cream (AgBr).
accept: Bromide gives a cream silver bromide precipitate after acidification and addition of silver nitrate.
reject: Bromide gives a white AgCl precipitate in the silver nitrate test.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What colour precipitate indicates iodide with silver ions?
records.originalBack: Yellow (AgI).
accept: Iodide gives a yellow AgI precipitate with acidified silver nitrate.
reject: Iodide produces a cream precipitate of AgBr in the silver nitrate test.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: When may initial rate be taken as proportional to 1/time?
records.originalBack: When each trial reaches the same small reaction extent at its timed endpoint.
accept: If every trial measures the same small conversion, shorter endpoint time implies a greater initial rate.
reject: The inverse of time is an initial-rate measure even when different trials stop at different reaction extents.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is a rate equation?
records.originalBack: An experimentally determined relationship between rate and reactant concentrations.
accept: An equation relating measured reaction rate to reactant concentrations with experimentally determined orders.
reject: The rate equation is obtained by reading coefficients off the balanced chemical equation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does the rate constant k depend on?
records.originalBack: Temperature, and any catalyst present.
accept: The rate constant depends on temperature and whether a catalyst is present.
reject: At fixed temperature and catalyst, k changes whenever a reactant concentration changes.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Does an exothermic reaction necessarily have zero activation energy?
records.originalBack: No; activation energy is a barrier, not the reaction's enthalpy change.
accept: Exothermic refers to negative reaction enthalpy; a separate activation-energy barrier can remain.
reject: An exothermic reaction must have zero energy barrier and proceed instantly.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does a catalyst do to activation energy?
records.originalBack: It provides an alternative route with lower activation energy.
accept: A catalyst allows a reaction pathway with lower activation energy.
reject: A catalyst makes a reaction faster by increasing activation energy.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Define Kp for a homogeneous gaseous equilibrium.
records.originalBack: The equilibrium constant expressed using the equilibrium partial pressures of the gases, at a fixed temperature.
accept: The equilibrium constant calculated from equilibrium partial gas pressures at one temperature.
reject: Kp uses the initial gas partial pressures instead of their equilibrium values.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Write Kp for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
records.originalBack: Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ [p(N₂) × p(H₂)³]. Use equilibrium partial pressures.
accept: For the Haber equilibrium, Kp=(pNH3)^2/((pN2)(pH2)^3).
reject: For N2+3H2 reversible 2NH3, Kp=(pN2)(pH2)^3/(pNH3)^2.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: When do the pressure units of Kp cancel?
records.originalBack: When the total gaseous coefficients are equal on both sides, so Δn = 0.
accept: Pressure powers cancel if the total gaseous mole coefficients on each side are equal.
reject: A Kp expression always has units of kPa irrespective of its gas coefficients.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Define lattice dissociation enthalpy.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic solid is completely separated into its constituent gaseous ions.
accept: The enthalpy change for breaking one mole of solid ionic lattice into separate gaseous ions.
reject: Lattice dissociation enthalpy is energy released when gaseous ions form an ionic solid.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Does a catalyst change ΔG or thermodynamic feasibility?
records.originalBack: No. A catalyst lowers activation energy and increases rate; it does not change ΔG for the overall reaction.
accept: It does not change Gibbs energy, only the reaction pathway and rate via a reduced activation barrier.
reject: Adding a catalyst changes equilibrium Gibbs energy and makes an infeasible reaction feasible.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How does increasing T affect ΔG when ΔS is positive versus negative?
records.originalBack: For ΔS > 0, ΔG decreases (more favourable). For ΔS < 0, ΔG increases (less favourable).
accept: If delta S>0, higher T lowers delta G; if delta S<0, higher T raises delta G, assuming delta H and delta S unchanged.
reject: Higher temperature always makes delta G smaller, regardless of the sign of delta S.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.section: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
records.originalFront: What does a larger Ka usually indicate?
records.originalBack: A stronger weak acid.
accept: A greater acid dissociation constant corresponds to greater dissociation and a stronger weak acid.
reject: For two comparable weak acids, the smaller Ka indicates the stronger acid.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is nucleophilic substitution?
records.originalBack: A nucleophile replaces another atom or group.
accept: It is a reaction where a nucleophile takes the place of a leaving atom or group.
reject: Nucleophilic substitution means adding a nucleophile without expelling any leaving group.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What distinguishes hydration from dehydration?
records.originalBack: Hydration adds water; dehydration removes it.
accept: Hydration adds the elements of water; dehydration eliminates the elements of water.
reject: Hydration removes water whereas dehydration adds it.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the functional group in an aldehyde?
records.originalBack: Terminal carbonyl group, –CHO.
accept: The aldehyde functional group is -CHO, a carbonyl at the end of a carbon chain.
reject: An aldehyde is a carbonyl between two carbon groups, RCO R'.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How is percentage titre uncertainty found?
records.originalBack: Absolute titre uncertainty ÷ titre ×100.
accept: Absolute uncertainty in the measured titre divided by titre, multiplied by 100 percent.
reject: Percentage titre uncertainty is the titre divided by absolute uncertainty times 100.
